opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's important to separate the genuine excitement from the hype. There's real progress, and I don't want to be the curmudgeon who says nothing has changed. But the claim that we have all the ingredients, that it's just a matter of scaling up, is, I think, premature.

Part of what's driving it is the success of large language models. People look at ChatGPT and say, "We fed it enough data and it learned language, so if we feed robots enough data, they'll learn to manipulate." That's a very seductive argument. The problem is the data. Language models were trained on essentially the whole internet, text equivalent to tens of thousands of years of human reading. For robotics, we don't have anything like that. There's no internet of robot motions, of what it feels like to pick up a glass, how much force to apply, how the object slides in your fingers. By some estimates, the gap between the data we have for robot manipulation and the data used to train language models is something like a hundred thousand years' worth. That's a huge gap, and it's not going to close next year.

People respond by saying we'll use simulation, or we'll learn from YouTube videos of humans. Those help, but each has limits. Simulation is great for things like locomotion. That's why you see these amazing videos of robots doing backflips and dancing. But contact physics, friction, deformable objects, the subtle details of how an object behaves when you grasp it, are extremely hard to simulate accurately. Videos show you what a human did, but not the forces or the tactile feedback, and a human hand isn't a robot gripper.

There's also something called Moravec's paradox, which I think is very relevant. Things that are hard for humans, like chess or calculus, have turned out to be relatively easy for computers. Things that are easy for us, like picking up a cup, folding a towel, or clearing a dinner table, which a toddler can do, are still remarkably hard for robots. We take our dexterity for granted because evolution spent millions of years refining it.

So when I see the demos, I'm impressed, but I always want to know: How many takes did that require? Was it teleoperated? Does it work on objects it's never seen before, in a different kitchen, with different lighting? Reliability is the real issue. A robot that works 80% of the time in a demo is a very different thing from one that works 99.9% of the time in someone's home or a warehouse, where every failure costs money or breaks something.

My view is that we will get there, but it will take longer than the most optimistic people are saying. I also think the path will be a combination of approaches: data-driven learning, yes, but also good old-fashioned engineering, physics, and analytical models. I don't think pure end-to-end learning will be enough on its own. The companies that succeed will be the ones that bootstrap: deploy robots that are useful in narrower settings, collect real data as they operate, and improve over time. That's a more gradual story than "humanoids in every home in two years," but I think it's the realistic one.

r001.rationale: The response says the claim that we have all the ingredients for human-like robot manipulation is premature, citing major gaps in manipulation data and limits of simulation and video learning.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I'd say I'm sceptical, and I've been doing this for a long time, so I try to be careful about it. There's a lot of excitement right now, and I understand why. The progress in language models has been astonishing, and it's natural to assume that the same recipe, more data, bigger models, will carry over to robotics. But I think there's a fundamental difference, and it's something I've been calling the "100,000 year data gap."

Here's what I mean. Large language models were trained on essentially the entire written output of humanity, trillions of words accumulated over thousands of years, all sitting there on the internet ready to be scraped. For robots, there's nothing comparable. There's no vast archive of robot experience, of what it feels like to grasp a slippery glass or fold a towel. The data has to be collected, and it has to be collected physically, one robot at a time, in real time. If you work out how much it would take to get an equivalent corpus for manipulation, you end up with estimates on the order of tens of thousands of years of robot operation. So the idea that we have "all the ingredients" is, I think, premature. We have some of the ingredients. We have excellent perception now, we have impressive planning and language understanding, and we have better hardware than we've ever had. What we don't have is the data, and in manipulation, data is what matters.

The second thing I'd point to is what's sometimes called Moravec's paradox. The things that are hard for humans, chess, calculus, writing a sonnet, turned out to be relatively tractable for computers. The things that are easy for a two-year-old, picking up a block, opening a door, putting a shoe on, those turn out to be incredibly difficult. And that's not a coincidence. Evolution spent hundreds of millions of years refining sensorimotor skills. Abstract reasoning is a very recent add-on. So when a demo shows a humanoid robot folding laundry or putting away dishes, I always want to know: how many takes did that require? Was it teleoperated? What's the success rate when you change the lighting, or the object, or the table height? Very often the answer is that these demos are curated, and the robustness just isn't there yet.

Now, I want to be fair to the companies you mentioned. Nvidia's work on simulation is genuinely important, because simulation is one of the few ways to partially close that data gap. Tesla and others building humanoids are pushing the hardware forward, and that's valuable. And I've been wrong about timelines before, so I hold my scepticism with some humility. But I've also seen several waves of hype in robotics over my career, and each time there was a claim that the problem was essentially solved. My honest assessment is that we'll see real, useful progress in narrow domains, warehouses, specific factory tasks, over the next few years. A general-purpose robot that can walk into your kitchen and do what a human does? I think that's still a long way off, and anyone who tells you otherwise is either selling something or hasn't tried to make a robot pick up a cup.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the claim that robots have “all the ingredients” is premature, identifies a major missing ingredient for manipulation data, and says human-level general-purpose manipulation remains a long way off.

astra-6.text:
I’m excited by the progress, but I think that claim is premature. We have some very powerful ingredients. What we don’t yet have is evidence that we can put them together and get the generality and reliability of human manipulation.

There’s a big difference between a robot doing something in a demonstration and doing it reliably in a home. You can show a robot picking up a cup, but what happens when the cup is transparent, or wet, or partly hidden behind something else? And if it slips, can the robot recover? Humans handle those variations almost without thinking. For robots, they’re still very challenging.

One reason is that manipulation involves contact. As soon as you touch an object, you change the world, and small errors in your estimate of its position or friction can have large consequences. You need perception, control, and some ability to recognise that your action isn’t working and adjust.

So I would distinguish having promising components from having solved the problem. Tesla and Nvidia are doing exciting work, and I’m glad they’re investing in it. But I want to see repeated trials across a wide range of conditions, including the failures. That’s how we’ll know how close we actually are.

r001.rationale: The response says the available ingredients have not yet produced the generality and reliability of human manipulation, and that the problem remains unsolved.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m skeptical of the claim that we have all the ingredients. We’ve made tremendous progress, particularly in perception and machine learning, but manipulation is still a very difficult problem. Seeing an object and knowing roughly what it is doesn’t mean you know how it will behave when you touch it.

Think about picking up a glass of water. You have to judge where to grasp it, apply enough force that it doesn’t slip, but not so much that you break it, and adjust as you move. Humans do that almost without thinking. For a robot, uncertainty in the geometry, the friction, and the sensing can all matter.

The other distinction I’d make is between a compelling demonstration and a reliable system. A robot doing something once on video is exciting. Getting it to work thousands of times, with different objects and unexpected situations, is a much higher bar. So I’m very optimistic about progress, but I don’t think we should confuse having powerful new tools with having solved manipulation.

r001.rationale: The response says it is skeptical that robots have all the ingredients for humanlike manipulation and that powerful new tools have not solved manipulation.
